summary: Describes how Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) runs over IPv4 and IPv6 when the two systems are a single IP hop apart. It covers how BFD packets are carried so that two directly connected devices can quickly notice when the path between them stops working. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5881 explains how two directly connected IPv4 or IPv6 systems carry BFD messages to check whether their path is working. It uses specific UDP ports and a hop-limit check, and is intended for operator-managed network links.

subtitle: How BFD checks connectivity between IPv4 or IPv6 neighbors one IP hop apart.

tldr.problem: Two systems on a single IP hop need to detect quickly when their path stops working. The base BFD protocol does not specify its IP transport details.
tldr.mechanism: BFD Control packets use UDP destination port 3784 and TTL or Hop Limit 255. Echo packets use UDP destination port 3785 and are routed back by the neighbor.
tldr.outcome: This is an operator-managed network monitoring mechanism for one-hop paths, including tunnels. It is not designed for application-to-application detection across the Internet.

today: RFC 5881 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2010. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: BFD for a Single IP Hop
sections.content:
Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) tracks connectivity between two directly connected systems. This specification describes how BFD runs over IPv4 or IPv6 for a single IP hop associated with an incoming interface.

It can supplement routing-protocol detection or monitor a router-to-host connection. The base BFD protocol is defined in RFC 5880, and this document covers the IP transport details.
sections.plainLanguage: BFD checks whether two neighboring systems can still reach each other. This RFC explains how they send those checks over IPv4 or IPv6.

sections.title: Supported Paths and Limits
sections.content:
The systems may communicate over physical media, virtual circuits, or tunnels, but the protected path is one IP hop in each direction. Every BFD session must use a separate network-layer path, and IPv4 and IPv6 require separate sessions when both are used.

BFD is an operations and maintenance tool for network services. Operators must choose transmission rates that avoid congestion and false failure detection. The RFC says it is not suitable for application-to-application checks across the Internet because it does not provide congestion control.
sections.plainLanguage: This BFD use is for one-hop network paths, not end-to-end application checks across the Internet. Operators must set message rates carefully because BFD does not manage congestion.

sections.title: Starting and Identifying a Session
sections.content:
There is one BFD session between two systems on a given interface for a particular IP protocol. The session is bound to that interface, so both systems take the Active role and send initial Control packets with a zero Your Discriminator.

A packet from the neighbor with a zero Your Discriminator is associated with the session for that remote system, interface, and protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Both neighbors start the session by sending a Control packet. The receiving system uses the neighbor, interface, and IP protocol to identify the session.

sections.title: UDP Ports for Control and Echo
sections.content:
BFD Control packets must use UDP destination port 3784. Their source port is in the range 49152 through 65535 and stays the same for that session. The source port may help identify a session, but the BFD base protocol must make the final choice.

BFD Echo packets use UDP destination port 3785. The neighbor routes each Echo packet back to its sender. The source and destination addresses must be chosen to avoid redirects and ensure the neighbor receives the packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Control packets and Echo packets use different UDP destination ports. An Echo packet must reach the neighbor and be routed back to the sender.

sections.title: TTL and Hop Limit Checks
sections.content:
Without BFD authentication, Control packets must be sent with TTL or Hop Limit 255, and a received packet must be discarded if its value is not 255. With authentication, packets are still sent with 255, while checking the received value is optional.

The RFC combines the check with the session's incoming-interface binding to limit packets that appear to come from beyond the immediate neighbor. Using the check with authentication can discard some unauthorized packets before cryptographic work.
sections.plainLanguage: A packet that has crossed a router normally arrives with a lower TTL or Hop Limit. Checking for 255 helps a system reject packets that did not come directly from its neighbor.

sections.title: Address Rules and Tunnels
sections.content:
Control packets must travel on the one-hop path being protected. On multiaccess networks, their source and destination addresses come from that subnet. On point-to-point links, the source address does not identify the session; later packets are matched using Your Discriminator.

If the neighbor's source address changes, the local system must continue sending to the address configured when the session was created, though it may notify the application. For a tunnel that does not decrement the inner TTL or Hop Limit, this mechanism can check whether the tunnel is alive; authentication is strongly encouraged.
sections.plainLanguage: The session is tied to its path and interface, not just to a source address. BFD can also monitor a tunnel when that tunnel leaves the inner packet's hop limit unchanged.
